tip: French says 'it makes' for weather: `il fait beau` (the weather's nice), `il fait froid`. Same pattern with `du soleil`, `du vent`. English uses 'be' or 'is sunny/windy'.
Passé composé = avoir or être + past participle. Most verbs take avoir: j'ai mangé, il a vu, nous avons fini. Usually no participle agreement.

target: Elle a mal à la tête.
tip: 'Avoir mal à' = to have pain in: j'ai mal au dos (my back hurts), j'ai mal aux dents (I have a toothache).
'Est-ce que' placed before a statement turns it into a yes/no question. It's the most common question form in spoken French.
'Demain' (tomorrow) is a time marker that doesn't change verb tense in questions – present tense works fine.
In inversion with 'il/elle', add -t- between two vowels: 'Parle-t-il ?' The -t- is just for pronunciation.
French negation wraps the verb: `je ne sais pas`. In speech the `ne` often drops (`je sais pas`) but it stays in writing. `Pas` alone after the verb is colloquial.
'De quoi' = What...of/about. Use after verbs that take 'de': avoir besoin de, parler de, avoir envie de.

target: Il n'y a pas de pain.
tip: After negation, 'du/de la/des' become 'de/d'': 'il y a du pain' → 'il n'y a pas de pain'.

target: Est-ce que nous sommes en retard ?
tip: In questions, 'est-ce que nous' sounds natural. The inverted form 'sommes-nous' is more formal.

target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
tip: 'Payer par carte' = to pay by card. 'Par' indicates the means of payment.
'Avoir hâte de' = to be eager to / can't wait to. Literally 'to have haste to'.
'Combien' = How much / How many. 'Combien ça coûte ?' is essential for shopping and travel.
When inverting with il/elle/on, add '-t-' between two vowels for pronunciation: A-t-il ? Va-t-elle ? Mange-t-on ?
'Lequel/laquelle' = Which one. Agrees with the noun: lequel (m.), laquelle (f.), lesquels (m. pl.), lesquelles (f. pl.).

english: I am afraid of the dog.
tip: 'Avoir peur de' = to be afraid of. Another 'avoir' expression where English uses 'to be'.
Regular past participles: -er → -é, -ir → -i, -re → -u. Irregulars (fait, dit, pris, lu, vu, eu, été) need separate memory.
'Avoir envie de' = to feel like / to want. J'ai envie d'un café = I feel like having a coffee.
'Arriver' uses 'être' in passé composé: 'je suis arrivé(e)'. 'En retard' = late. Regular -er in present.
After negation, 'des' becomes 'd'' before a vowel: 'pas d'amis'. The partitive article disappears.
'Vieux' has special forms: vieux (m. before consonant), vieil (m. before vowel), vieille (f.), vieux (m. pl.), vieilles (f. pl.).

target: Je suis fatigué après le travail.
tip: Use 'être' for states and conditions: je suis fatigué (I am tired), je suis content (I am happy).

target: Une vieille dame lit le journal.
english: An old lady reads the newspaper.
tip: 'Le/la/les' for general statements: 'J'aime le chocolat' = I like chocolate (in general).

target: Les magasins ferment à vingt heures.
english: The stores close at eight pm.
tip: 'Les magasins' – use 'les' for all/general plural nouns. 'Des' would mean 'some' stores.

target: Est-ce qu'il y a un parking ?
tip: 'Est-ce qu'il y a' = Is there / Are there. 'Il y a' means 'there is/are' and is very common.

target: À quelle heure tu te lèves ?
english: What time do you get up?
tip: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun (me/te/se/nous/vous/se) before the verb. `Je m'appelle` = 'I call myself' = 'My name is'. The pronoun must match the subject.

target: Ils ont un chien et un chat.
english: They have a dog and a cat.
tip: 'Être pressé' = to be in a hurry. The adjective agrees: pressé/pressée.

target: Comment on va à la gare ?
english: How do we get to the station?
tip: `on` also = English 'one' or 'they' (impersonal): `on dit que...` = 'they say that...'. Two meanings, one word. Context decides.

target: Un café et un croissant, s'il vous plaît.
english: A coffee and a croissant, please.
tip: 'Un café et un croissant' – 'un/une' are indefinite articles. Use them when ordering one of something.
'Comment' = How/What. 'Comment tu t'appelles ?' is informal. Formal: 'Comment vous appelez-vous ?'
'Pourquoi' = Why. Can be followed by subject+verb directly or by 'est-ce que': Pourquoi est-ce que tu ris ?
In casual French, you can put the question word at the end: Tu viens d'où ? Tu fais quoi ? C'est qui ?
'La' is the feminine singular definite article. Use 'la' before feminine nouns starting with a consonant: la maison, la table, la rue.
'Les' is the plural definite article for both masculine and feminine nouns: les garçons, les filles, les maisons.
'Bon' (m.) → 'bonne' (f.) = good. Most adjectives add -e for feminine: petit → petite, grand → grande.
Possessives: ton/ta/tes (your, informal). Before feminine nouns starting with a vowel, use 'mon/ton/son' instead of 'ma/ta/sa': mon amie.
More elisions: ne → n', me → m', te → t', se → s', le/la → l', de → d', que → qu'. Any vowel collision triggers it.
'Chaud' (m.) → 'chaude' (f.) = hot. 'Froid' → 'froide' = cold. Regular feminine form: just add -e.
'Gros' (m.) → 'grosse' (f.) = big/fat. Multiple adjectives: size before noun + color after: un gros chien noir.
'Leur' is the indirect object pronoun for 'them': 'ce restaurant leur plaît' = this restaurant pleases them.
'Qu'est-ce qui' = What (as subject). Use when 'what' is doing the action: Qu'est-ce qui fait ce bruit ? (What's making that noise?)
'Une bière' is feminine. Most drinks ending in -ère are feminine: une bière, une rivière.
'Qu'est-ce que' = What (as object of verb). Use for 'what' questions: Qu'est-ce que tu veux ? (What do you want?)
The inverted question form 'parlez-vous' is more formal than 'est-ce que vous parlez'. Both are correct.
'Lequel/laquelle' = which one. Agrees in gender and number: lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles.
'À qui' = to whom / whose: 'À qui est ce livre ?' = Whose book is this?
'De la' is the feminine partitive article meaning 'some'. Use for feminine uncountable nouns: de la salade, de la soupe, de la viande.
'De' replaces partitives after negation, but not after 'ne...que' (only): 'Je ne bois que du café'.
'Long' (m.) → 'longue' (f.) = long. Irregular feminine form. Some adjectives change more than just adding -e.
'Il me faut' = I need (literally: it is necessary to me). Reverse construction: il me faut, il te faut, il lui faut, il nous faut.
'Suffire' (to be enough) is impersonal like falloir: 'il suffit de' = it's enough to.
Negative pairs: ne … jamais (never), ne … plus (no longer), ne … rien (nothing), ne … personne (no one). Always two parts around the verb.

target: Il y a du vent aujourd'hui.
tip: 'Du/de la/des' for partial quantities: 'Je mange du pain' = I eat some bread (not all bread).
'Où' (where) with accent distinguishes it from 'ou' (or) without accent. The accent matters in writing.
After a negation, the article switches: `j'ai un chien` → `je n'ai pas de chien`. The `un/une/des` becomes `de`. Very easy to forget for English speakers.
'Quand' = When. Use with 'est-ce que' or inversion: Quand pars-tu ? / Quand est-ce que tu pars ?

target: Je ne mange jamais de viande.
tip: 'Ne...jamais de' = never any. Same rule: un/une/du/de la become 'de' in negative: Je ne bois jamais de café.

target: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
tip: 'C'est gentil' = that's kind. A common way to thank someone for their thoughtfulness.
'Quel/quelle' (which/what) agrees with the noun: quel livre (m.), quelle heure (f.), quels jours (m.pl.).

target: Il y a trop de bruit.
tip: `il y a` = 'there is / there are' – singular and plural. `Il y a une pomme`, `il y a trois pommes`. The form doesn't change. Past: `il y avait`.
